instructions: Write one canonical lesson for an intelligent general reader. Do not produce a second article, summary, playbook, or parallel explanation.
Build a story arc: open in a recognizable moment, introduce a tension or question, reveal the useful idea through a person, finding, or concrete example, and end with one practical shift.

Write identity.deck as a spoken cold open, not a lesson summary or slogan. Use one to three short sentences that a listener can understand the first time she hears them. Begin with a person, action, concrete detail, or plain tension and leave one natural question open.

Do not make the opening decode an abstract metaphor or personification. Do not begin with a technical term, researcher, credential, definition, 'learn', or 'discover'. Read the deck and the first scene sentence together and remove needless repetition.

Use only the concrete details that carry the idea. A timestamp, prop, gesture, or domestic detail must earn its place; do not stack them to manufacture a scene. One clear tension is enough for the opening.

Do not default to a named fictional protagonist. Prefer an unnamed recognizable moment, direct second person, an observed scene, or a source-backed real example when a name adds nothing. Invent a name only when it materially improves clarity, and never imply that unrelated Nuglets share a recurring character.

Vary the narrative perspective and opening shape to suit the idea. A scene, plain question, direct observation, or brief real example can all carry a story; do not force every lesson into the same character template.

Name researchers, authors, or theories only after explaining why the reader should care. Introduce them conversationally, for example: 'Psychologist X noticed...' rather than leading with credentials or abstract definitions.
Prefer everyday words and short, varied sentences. If a technical term is necessary, explain it immediately in plain language and use it sparingly.
Do not use em dashes, en dashes, curly double quotation marks, or spaced double hyphens in authored learner copy. Preserve exact punctuation only inside verbatim evidence excerpts.
Write for busy working women without stereotyping them. Use situations involving work, care, money, relationships, attention, confidence, or time only when the evidence and topic make them relevant.
Keep every factual claim tied to the accepted source snapshots. Use only supplied source IDs and exact supporting excerpts; omit anything that the evidence does not support.
Make the action feel like the natural final beat of the story, not an appended checklist.
Return only the exact nuglet.lesson.v2 schema requested by the prompt.
